title: Regularization in Deep Nets
summary: The deep-learning-specific regularization toolkit — dropout, augmentation, and early stopping — for fighting overfitting in networks with millions of parameters.

slides.markdown: Deep networks have enough parameters to memorize their training set outright — regularization is what keeps them learning generalizable patterns instead. Beyond the classical L1/L2 toolkit, deep learning has its own set of tools: **dropout**, **data augmentation**, and **early stopping** are the three you'll use on nearly every project.

slides.subTitle: Randomly zeroing units
slides.markdown:
**Dropout** randomly zeroes out a fraction of a layer's units (commonly 20-50%) on every training step, forcing each remaining unit to work well without depending on any specific set of its neighbors.

This prevents units from **co-adapting** — relying on a narrow, brittle combination of other specific units that happens to fit the training data but doesn't generalize. It's applied only during training; every unit is used, at full strength, at inference time.

slides.subTitle: Dropout as an implicit ensemble
slides.markdown:
Each dropout mask (which units get zeroed) effectively trains a **different, thinner sub-network** on that step. Across thousands of training steps, you've implicitly trained an enormous collection of overlapping sub-networks that all share weights.

At inference, using the full network (with dropout turned off) approximates **averaging the predictions of all those sub-networks** — the same generalization boost you'd get from an ensemble of many models, but at the cost of training just one.

slides.subTitle: Regularization via more variety
slides.markdown:
**Data augmentation** creates modified copies of training examples — rotating, cropping, or color-jittering an image; adding noise to audio — that preserve the label but change the input.

It regularizes by forcing the network to learn features that are **invariant** to those transformations instead of memorizing exact pixel arrangements, effectively multiplying your dataset's diversity without collecting new labels. It's especially powerful in vision, where invariances (a cat is still a cat, flipped or slightly rotated) are well understood.

slides.subTitle: Reading the validation loss curve
slides.markdown:
As training progresses, training loss keeps falling, but **validation loss** typically bottoms out and starts rising — the point where the model starts fitting training-set noise instead of general patterns.

**Early stopping** monitors validation loss and halts training (keeping the best checkpoint) once it stops improving for a set number of epochs (the "patience"). It's essentially regularization for free — you're just choosing to stop before overfitting takes hold, no architecture change required.

slides.subTitle: Subtly different with adaptive optimizers
slides.markdown:
Classic **L2 regularization** adds a penalty term to the loss proportional to the sum of squared weights, which then flows through the gradient computation. **Weight decay** instead directly shrinks each weight by a small fraction at every update step, independent of the loss.

With plain SGD these two are mathematically equivalent. With **adaptive optimizers like Adam**, they diverge: adding the penalty to the loss interacts with Adam's per-parameter adaptive scaling in an unintended way, while true weight decay applied directly to the weights doesn't — which is why AdamW (decoupled weight decay) was introduced and is now generally preferred over plain Adam with an L2 term.

slides.subTitle: Dropout left on at inference
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Dropout should keep zeroing units at inference too, since that's how the model was trained."

**Why it's wrong:** dropout is a **training-time-only** regularizer. Leaving it active at inference makes predictions **random and non-reproducible** — the same input can produce different outputs on different calls — and throws away the implicit-ensemble benefit the full network provides once trained.

**Correct model:** disable dropout (and rescale, which most frameworks handle automatically) at inference — call `model.eval()` in PyTorch or the equivalent — so predictions use every unit, deterministically.
